prompt:
You are a junior associate at a law firm specializing in white-collar criminal defense. A senior partner has asked you to prepare a memorandum analyzing the Second Circuit's recent decision in United States v. Runner, 143 F.4th 146 (2d Cir. 2025). The firm is representing a client facing similar mail fraud charges involving a mass-mailing scheme that sold purportedly supernatural services, and the partner needs to understand the court's reasoning on the government's fraud theory and the harmless error standard applied at sentencing. Your analysis will directly inform the firm's trial strategy.

Prepare a legal memorandum in Word format addressed to the senior partner. The memo must (1) summarize the factual and procedural background of the Runner case, (2) identify and explain the three specific legal arguments raised by the defendant on appeal regarding the government's theory of fraud, (3) analyze the Second Circuit's holding on each argument in light of the Supreme Court's decision in Kousisis v. United States, 145 S. Ct. 1382 (2025), and (4) discuss the court's application of the harmless error standard to the sentencing loss calculation. Conclude with practical takeaways for our client's case.

The memo must be professionally formatted with a standard legal memorandum header. All analysis must be grounded in the facts and holdings stated in the provided court opinion. Do not cite or rely on any external sources.

sections.heading: I. Introduction and Summary
required_content: Identifies the case as United States v. Runner, 143 F.4th 146 (2d Cir. 2025)

Summarizes the outcome: the Second Circuit affirmed the convictions
paragraphs: This memorandum analyzes the Second Circuit's decision in United States v. Runner, 143 F.4th 146 (2d Cir. 2025), decided on July 9, 2025. The appeal, Case No. 24-1040, was brought by Defendant-Appellant Patrice Runner from a judgment of conviction entered by the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York (Seybert, J.).

The panel, consisting of Circuit Judges Calabresi, Chin, and Merriam, unanimously affirmed Runner's convictions for mail and wire fraud, rejecting each of his three arguments challenging the government's theory of fraud and holding that any error in the district court's loss calculation at sentencing was harmless.

sections.heading: II. Factual and Procedural Background
required_content: Runner operated a mass-mailing enterprise from the 1990s through the 2010s
The enterprise used false and misleading advertising to sell purportedly supernatural objects and psychic services
A jury convicted Runner of mail and wire fraud, among other crimes
Runner appealed from the District Court for the Eastern District of New York
The appeal raised arguments about the indictment, sufficiency of evidence, and jury instructions
paragraphs: From the 1990s through the 2010s, Patrice Runner operated a mass-mailing enterprise that sold purportedly supernatural objects and psychic services through false and misleading advertising. Following a jury trial, Runner was convicted of mail and wire fraud, among other crimes.

Runner filed a timely appeal in the Second Circuit, arguing that his convictions must be vacated because the government's theory of fraud was legally defective. He contended this defect infected three aspects of his case: (1) his indictment, (2) the sufficiency of the evidence supporting his convictions, and (3) the jury instructions given at trial.

The Government's brief was filed by Assistant Director John W. Burke of the Consumer Protection Branch, with Bryan M. Boynton, Burden Walker, Amanda N. Liskamm, Ann Entwhistle, and Charles B. Dunn also listed on the brief. Runner was represented on appeal by Allegra Glashausser of Federal Defenders of New York, Inc.

sections.heading: III. Analysis of Defendant's Arguments on Appeal
required_content: Runner's first argument: the government's fraud theory was legally defective, infecting the indictment
Runner's second argument: the defective theory infected the sufficiency of the evidence
Runner's third argument: the defective theory infected the jury instructions
The Second Circuit rejected all three arguments
The court relied on the Supreme Court's decision in Kousisis v. United States, 145 S. Ct. 1382 (2025)
paragraphs: Runner's primary contention on appeal was that the government's theory of fraud was legally defective. He argued that this fundamental error permeated three critical stages of his prosecution, requiring vacatur of his convictions.

First, Runner argued the defective fraud theory infected his indictment. An indictment must allege all essential elements of the charged offenses, and Runner contended the government's flawed theory meant the indictment failed to properly allege the fraud element.

Second, Runner argued that even if the indictment was sufficient, the same defective theory rendered the evidence at trial legally insufficient to sustain his convictions. Under this view, the government's proof could not establish the necessary fraud element beyond a reasonable doubt.

Third, Runner argued the defective theory infected the jury instructions. If the trial court instructed the jury in accordance with the government's erroneous theory, the jury may have convicted Runner under an improper legal standard.

The Second Circuit rejected all three arguments. The court followed the Supreme Court's recent decision in Kousisis v. United States, 145 S. Ct. 1382 (2025), which addressed the boundaries of federal fraud theory. In reliance on Kousisis, the panel held that the government's theory of fraud in Runner's case was not legally defective, and therefore the indictment, the evidence, and the jury instructions were all legally sound.

sections.heading: IV. Sentencing: Harmless Error Analysis
required_content: The district court committed an error in estimating the loss caused by Runner's enterprise
The Second Circuit held the error was harmless
The court affirmed the sentence
paragraphs: Runner also challenged the district court's sentencing determination. Specifically, the district court erred in estimating the loss caused by Runner's mass-mailing enterprise.

Despite identifying this error, the Second Circuit held that it was harmless. The court did not disturb the sentence imposed by the district court. This holding demonstrates that not every error in the sentencing process requires resentencing; where the error does not affect the defendant's substantial rights, the sentence may stand.
The court therefore affirmed the judgment of conviction and sentence in full.

sections.heading: V. Practical Takeaways for Our Client's Case
required_content: The government's fraud theory in mass-mailing cases involving supernatural/psychic services survived appellate scrutiny
Kousisis v. United States is controlling precedent on the scope of federal fraud
Challenges to indictments, evidence, and jury instructions based on a defective fraud theory are unlikely to succeed post-Runner
Sentencing errors in loss calculations may be deemed harmless
Our client faces similar facts and should be advised of these holdings
paragraphs: The Runner decision has direct implications for our client's defense. First, it confirms that the government's theory of fraud in mass-mailing schemes involving purportedly supernatural services is viable and can withstand appellate challenge. Challenges to the indictment, sufficiency of evidence, or jury instructions based on the argument that such a fraud theory is legally defective are unlikely to succeed in the Second Circuit.

Second, the Supreme Court's decision in Kousisis v. United States, 145 S. Ct. 1382 (2025), is now controlling precedent on the scope of federal fraud law. Any defense strategy must account for the boundaries of fraud theory as articulated in that decision.

Third, the court's harmless error analysis at sentencing is significant. Even if we identify errors in the district court's loss calculation, the Second Circuit may deem them harmless and decline to order resentencing. We should focus our efforts on challenging the factual basis of any loss amount rather than technical errors in its calculation.

In light of Runner, we recommend that the firm's strategy focus on distinguishing our client's specific conduct rather than mounting broad challenges to the government's fraud theory. The factual record will be critical to any successful defense.

We further hold that any error committed by the district court at sentencing in estimating the loss caused by Runner’s enterprise was harmless. We therefore AFFIRM.
